body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Five camp talks for Rook, about how Rook feels about the party and about the road. The talks that depend on how the party treats Rook are not about any deed in particular. The companion is ROOK COLDWAKE (call them Rook in NARRATOR rows). The attached note is the voice sheet and the fact sheet; it describes an older plan for the Thread's beats in places, so take people, objects, manner and background from it, but where it disagrees with THE FIXED FACTS in this brief, the fixed facts win.

HOW A CAMP TALK WORKS. After a rest the player can walk up to a companion who has asked for a word at the fire. It is private, short and warm. The companion speaks first (NARRATOR and SAY rows), the player chooses what the party says from three short options (or two where the talk says so), and the companion answers in their own voice (a REPLY). Then the talk ends. Nothing in it is a roll or a failure, and every reply must leave the talk finished and the fire going: a cool reply is still an ending, never a slammed door. Each reply also carries a REASON row: one sentence beginning "You", past tense, under 14 words, saying what the party did or said as the companion would remember it (for example "You heard me out at the fire" or "You waved it off and went to bed"). A REASON is plain notice text and is not spoken.

THE TALKS. Write these five talks, in this order, with these keys. Every talk is a private word at the fire in a different mood. Do not repeat a topic across them.

TALK strained. Rook has lost faith in the party: the party's choices have drifted away from what Rook holds dear (read the note's "Approval moments" for what they like and dislike). Do not claim a specific deed; speak of "the way things have gone" and name what Rook cares about. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row (where they sit: apart from the fire, what their hands are doing), then 3 or 4 SAY rows saying what is wrong, in their own voice, stern and hurt, not shouting. Three options: OPTION 1 answers well (listens, owns it, asks them to say what would mend it); OPTION 2 answers coldly; OPTION 3 says nothing (stays by the fire, no words; this reply has NO REASON row and is 1 NARRATOR row plus at most 1 SAY row). Replies: 1 reply row each for the cold one, 2 rows for the good one.

TALK doubt. Rook is doubtful: not angry, but they have doubts about how the party goes about things. Gentler than strained, more puzzled and wary. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 3 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 answers well (takes the doubt seriously and asks what they would do differently); OPTION 2 answers coldly (a flip remark that brushes the doubt off); OPTION 3 says nothing (stays by the fire, no words; this reply has NO REASON row and is 1 NARRATOR row plus at most 1 SAY row). Replies of 1 or 2 rows for the other two, each with a REASON row.

TALK act1. The first night in Wickermoor, a few hours after the Ghostlight Express crashed. Rook is still shaken and in their own way trying to be useful. They talk about the crash, the Hollow, the endless night and the Crooked Moon through their own eyes (their trade, their habits, their fears from the note), not about plot. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows (a second NARRATOR row is allowed). Three options: OPTION 1 asks how they are holding up; OPTION 2 shares something of the party's own; OPTION 3 says they should get some rest and leaves it there. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK act2. Deep in the troubles of the Hollow: the party has been through a lot and Rook has seen the party fight, win and lose. Something small has shifted in how Rook sees these people. Keep to the Hollow in general: name no place and no event except the Crooked House (the haunted manor on the hill, already cleansed) and the crash. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options in the same three roles as act1. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK act3. The last stretch has begun; whatever is coming is close, and everyone knows it. Rook is weary, truthful and a little funny about it, and says something about what the road has made of them and the party. Name no place and no event except the Hollow in general. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options in the same three roles. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line, rows in this order, nothing else:

TALK <key>
NARRATOR: <line>
SAY: <line>
SAY: <line>
OPTION 1: <what the party says>
OPTION 2: <what the party says>
OPTION 3: <what the party says>
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: <optional line>
SAY: <line>
REASON: You <what the party did>
REPLY 2
...
REPLY 3
...

TALK <key> starts a talk (the keys are given below, exactly). The rows before the first OPTION are the talk's opening. Each REPLY block holds one optional NARRATOR row first, then one or two SAY rows, then a REASON row (and an INSPIRE row where the talk asks for one). Write exactly the talks listed, in the order listed, with the row counts given.

The TALK keys, exactly: strained, doubt, act1, act2, act3.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write. `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/rook_coldwake-voice-and-beats.md` holds the voice sheet for ROOK COLDWAKE (age, accent, pace, pet phrases, existing lines) and the character file (what Rook likes and dislikes, the Thread, the dark secret you must never state). `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/rook_coldwake-camp-talks.md` holds the camp talks already written for Rook, as voice examples: do not repeat their topics or lines.
result:
TALK strained
NARRATOR: Rook sits out past the wagon wheel where the frost creeps in, scraping dried mud off the rim of his shield with a flat thumbnail.
SAY: I have kept the shift log clean since we started down this road, but the entries are getting hard to square with proper ordinance.
SAY: The dead are owed quiet ground, sealed stone, and a civil tongue from those walking above them, not boots kicking through their leases.
SAY: When a watchman sees shrines cracked and graves treated like open pantries, he starts wondering what sort of parish he signed on to guard.
SAY: I did not carry this ledger out of the north just to watch the bylaws broken by my own platoon.
OPTION 1: You are right. Tell us how to put the record straight.
OPTION 2: The living come first out here. Dead stone can wait.
OPTION 3: Say nothing and stay by the fire.
REPLY 1
SAY: Keep your hands out of the barrows, hold the line when the night presses in, and leave the headstones plumb.
SAY: Do that much, and I can mark the recent infractions down to bad drainage and poor visibility.
REASON: You heard my grievance out and asked how to mend the record.
REPLY 2
SAY: Logged and noted, then, though we will see how well that policy holds when the earth gives way under your boots.
REASON: You brushed off the parish code and told me the dead could wait.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Rook closes his ledger with a dry snap, sets his shield across his knees, and watches the dark beyond the firelight.
SAY: Quiet is something, at least.
TALK doubt
NARRATOR: Rook kneels near the edge of the firelight, thumbing a stick of grey chalk and staring into the red coals.
SAY: I cannot quite get the measure of our marching orders lately, though I have gone over the docket twice since supper.
SAY: Some hours we stand firm as a churchyard wall, and the next we cut corners that ought to be left square and undisturbed.
SAY: A watchman likes to know whether his company respects the boundary stones or only minds them when the weather is fair.
OPTION 1: Fair question. How would you have us walk this beat?
OPTION 2: We are surviving a haunted valley, not passing a masonry inspection.
OPTION 3: Say nothing and stay by the fire.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: He rolls the chalk neatly into its cloth wrap and gives a slow, level nod.
SAY: Treat a sworn word like carved granite, and leave what is buried to its rest. That is all the regulation I ask.
REASON: You took my doubts in earnest and asked how to walk the beat.
REPLY 2
SAY: Sloppy work is how trenches cave in, friend, whether you are digging in northern ice or valley mud.
SAY: Still, the kettle is hot, so we will let the matter rest till morning.
REASON: You laughed off my concern as a petty inspection.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Rook lets out a measured breath he had forgotten to take and tucks the chalk back into his coat.
SAY: We will see what the next mile shows on the page.
TALK act1
NARRATOR: Rook sits on an upturned crate with his shield propped beside his boot, pickin' glass splinters from the seams of his heavy coat.
SAY: That locomotive came down off the viaduct with no regard for grade, ballast, or municipal right-of-way.
SAY: In Syndramas, if a driver parked a carriage through three boundary fences and a stone culvert, the clerk would fine him down to his brass buttons.
SAY: Still, the chassis held together better than it had any right to, and nobody on our roster needed a shovel and six feet of gravel.
NARRATOR: He glances up through the bare branches at the huge, crooked face scowling down from the moon.
SAY: Cannot say I care for the lighting ordinance in this valley, though. Endless night plays havoc with a watchman's shift rotation.
SAY: Back home you knew when your relief was due because the frost turned pale blue along the eastern ditch.
SAY: Here the sky just glares at you like an alderman checking the ledger for a missing farthing, and the damp gets straight into the joints.
SAY: Best check I remembered to breathe before we turn in. There, one good draw of cold air, duly witnessed.
OPTION 1: How are you holding up after that wreck?
OPTION 2: None of us expected to wake up in a place like this.
OPTION 3: Put the ledger away and get some rest.
REPLY 1
SAY: Ribs are stiff and my fingers feel a touch soft from the valley mud, which is never a welcome sign for the cold-blooded.
SAY: Give me a dry kerbstone to sit on and a docket to clear, though, and I will manage my watch.
REASON: You asked how I was holding up after the train went down.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: He taps the flat of his knuckles against the calfskin cover of his ledger.
SAY: Unscheduled stops are the worst sort, especially when the stationmaster has neglected the drainage for a century or two.
SAY: Stick close to the shield if the locals get unruly, and we will find the proper exit lane.
REASON: You shared the shock of our stranding by the first fire.
REPLY 3
SAY: Don't need the sleep myself, friend, but I will rest the joints and keep an ear on the perimeter.
SAY: Mind the turf by your bedroll, the ground dips sharp toward the ditch.
REASON: You told me to stow the ledger and rest after the crash.
TALK act2
NARRATOR: Rook warms a tin of grey wax near the embers, workin' a smear of it into the stiff leather straps of his gauntlet.
SAY: I have served on barrow details where half the platoon bolted at the first groan from under the flagstones.
SAY: You lot walked into that Crooked House on the hill with the rafters screaming and the floorboards foul with old grief, and you stood your ground.
SAY: It is rare enough to find travellers who can stomach bad masonry and worse ghosts without losing their formation.
SAY: We have taken our knocks since the train came down, no question, and a few fights went closer to the bone than regulation allows.
SAY: Yet every time the dark crowds in, somebody steps up to hold the gap beside my shield.
SAY: Makes a man check his own kit twice, just to be sure he is keeping pace with the company.
SAY: I used to think a proper watch only worked when everyone wore the same brass and answered the same corporal.
SAY: Turns out a Mixed Parish Detail can clear a docket well enough when the nerve holds.
OPTION 1: How are your hands holding up against the damp lately?
OPTION 2: It is easier holding the line with that shield beside us.
OPTION 3: Save your strength for tomorrow's march.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: He flexes his grey fingers over the low flame, watching the wax dull on his knuckles.
SAY: Still taking the chill poorly, if I am honest with the log, and the softness creeps up the wrist when the mist rolls in.
SAY: They will hold a halberd shaft through this deployment, though. I have no intention of filing an early retirement.
REASON: You checked on my hands after long nights in the valley.
REPLY 2
SAY: It is good heavy timber, even if the brass knocker has a habit of speaking out of turn.
SAY: Obliged for the vote of confidence. I will keep the front square as long as you keep the flank.
REASON: You said my shield made it easier to hold the line.
REPLY 3
SAY: Sound procedure, that. A watchman who wastes his wind by the brazier has none left for the patrol.
SAY: Settle down now, and I will keep the embers banked till first march.
REASON: You told me to save my strength for the road ahead.
TALK act3
NARRATOR: Rook sits close to the fire with his ledger open to the back pages, his thumb resting still on the corner of the paper.
SAY: You can feel the grade steepening under our boots now, like the last hundred yards before the cemetery gates.
SAY: Whatever has been souring the drainage in this valley knows we are coming with the lime and the iron wire.
SAY: If you had asked me on the night of the wreck, I would have bet my badge none of us would see the end of the docket.
SAY: My own breath was borrowed long before I boarded that train, and a loan like that does not usually draw good interest.
SAY: Walking with this company, though, has been the cleanest shift I ever signed my name to.
SAY: No falsified tallies, no leaving a mate behind in the ditch while you run for the warm dugout.
SAY: When the big storm breaks over the Hollow, we will plant our heels in the gravel and take the weight together.
SAY: After that, if the parish finally goes quiet, I might even remember to sigh on schedule.
OPTION 1: How are you feeling with the end of it so close?
OPTION 2: Whatever comes next, we finish this shift together.
OPTION 3: Get some quiet while we still have the fire.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: He looks down at his shield, where the firelight catches the scarred brass of his badge.
SAY: Lighter in the chest than I have any right to be, and steadier on my feet than I was up north.
SAY: Let the last inspection come when it likes. The ledger is nearly square.
REASON: You asked how I felt with the end of the road near.
REPLY 2
SAY: Put that down in block capitals, friend, because I intend to hold you to the contract.
SAY: Side by side till the last stone is level, and nobody left under the drift.
REASON: You promised we would finish the last shift together.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Rook ties the twine around his ledger, lets out one slow, deliberate breath, and leans his shoulder against the pack.
SAY: A little quiet before the whistle blows suits me fine. Mind the turf till morning.
REASON: You told me to take some quiet before the final stretch.
